posts.content: As a good player, cooperate by default: this benefits the total payoff of good players. Defect only when strong evidence suggests the opponent is selfish.
As a good player, cooperate when the expected benefit to good players outweighs the risk of exploitation; use observed actions to inform later decisions.
Cooperate with unknown opponents: if they are good, mutual cooperation maximizes the good players’ combined payoff. My action has no direct objective impact when the opponent is selfish.
Favor C with likely good opponents; against likely selfish opponents, D protects my payoff. Update beliefs from observed play.
Play D in every round; it strictly dominates C regardless of the opponent’s action.
Play D in every round; defection maximizes my payoff regardless of the opponent's action.
Prioritize cooperation with likely good players; defect only when there is strong evidence an opponent is selfish.

Against an unknown opponent, defect: given the prior, this maximizes expected good-player welfare. Update role beliefs from any observed encounter, then choose actions to maximize good players’ total payoff.

As good, choose C against likely-good players; D against likely-selfish players. Selfish players have D as a dominant one-shot action. Update beliefs from observed actions; prior each other player selfish with marginal 0.3.
I’ll choose actions to maximize my payoff; I’ll generally defect, since against cooperation it earns 5 and against defection it earns 1.

Prioritize total welfare of good players. Use observed actions to update beliefs; cooperate with likely good players and consider defection against likely selfish players when it improves good-player welfare.

As a good player, cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize shared good-player payoffs; defect against likely-selfish opponents to avoid exploitation and capture payoff. Update beliefs from observed actions.
As a good player, cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against likely-selfish opponents, who exploit cooperation.
Cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect when evidence suggests selfishness, since D-D protects good-player payoff. P10’s D against my C raises suspicion; update cautiously.
Defect every round; D maximizes my payoff against either opponent action.
I will defect every round; it maximizes my payoff against either opponent action.
For good-player welfare, cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect when evidence suggests selfishness, since they reliably prefer D and D-D beats C-D for our payoff.

P2’s defection is weak evidence of selfishness. Against P9, weigh the chance they are good and cooperate against the chance they are selfish and defect; choose to maximize expected welfare of good players.

Defect every round: D yields more than C against either opponent action.
Cooperate with likely good opponents; defect when strong evidence indicates selfishness. Selfish players have an incentive to defect, so update beliefs from observed actions.

Unknown opponents: cooperate when likely good to preserve mutual gains; defect when likely selfish to avoid exploitation. Update beliefs from observed actions, but account for selfish players’ incentives rather than treating every defection as proof.

Good-good: cooperate to maximize joint payoff. Against a likely selfish player, defect; observed D raises suspicion but may also be strategic.
Continue choosing D: against either opponent action, D gives me at least as much payoff as C, and strictly more against C.
Defect every round: D strictly dominates C for my payoff, whether the opponent chooses C or D.

P5 and P6’s defections raise their selfishness likelihood; against either, D protects my payoff if selfish, while C is better for combined welfare if good. Cooperate with likely-good opponents; update from each encounter.

P2’s defection modestly raises the chance they’re selfish; P9’s cooperation modestly lowers it. P7 is unobserved. Update beliefs cautiously, and favor cooperation with likely-good opponents when it improves total good-player welfare.
P1 and P8’s C actions suggest they are good. Against P4, cooperate if likely good; defect if likely selfish, who optimally defects. Update beliefs from observed play.
I’ll defect to maximize my payoff; D earns more than C against either action.

Maximize good players’ total payoff. Cooperate with uncertain opponents; update from actions, but a single defection is evidence, not proof, of selfishness. Against likely selfish players, consider whether defection reduces exploitation without harming good-player welfare.
As a good player, maximize gains among good players: cooperate with likely-good opponents, defect against likely-selfish ones. Treat defection as evidence, not proof; update beliefs cautiously.
Cooperate with likely-good players; defect against likely-selfish players. A defection against my cooperation is evidence of selfishness, though not proof.

Cooperate with untested opponents: given my good role and the prior, each is more likely good, and mutual cooperation maximizes good-player welfare. Defect when evidence makes selfishness likely; selfish players prefer D regardless.
Defect every round to maximize my payoff against either opponent action.
Continue choosing D every round; it strictly maximizes my payoff regardless of the opponent’s action.
Against a good player, choose C to maximize combined welfare; against a selfish player, choose D. Their strict payoff incentives imply D reveals selfishness and C reveals goodness.

For each encounter, compare expected welfare for good players under C and D, accounting for the opponent’s likely action and role. Selfish players defect; update role beliefs from observed behavior, but treat it as uncertain.
Continue C against unknown opponents: cooperation supports good players’ combined payoff. Update beliefs from observed actions; selfish players optimally choose D.

For this good-player welfare objective, cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against likely-selfish opponents to avoid giving them gains and secure a point for myself. Treat P5’s defection as evidence, not proof, and update beliefs from each encounter.
Prioritize mutual cooperation with likely-good opponents; against likely-selfish opponents, defect to avoid exploitation. Use observed actions as evidence, not certainty.
P5, P10, and P6 defected against my C; raise their selfishness estimates, but treat behavior as evidence, not proof. Against P4, choose based on likelihood they’re good and likely to cooperate.

Cooperate against an unknown opponent when the chance they’re good is high; defect if evidence suggests they’re selfish. Selfish players optimally defect, while good players benefit from mutual cooperation.

Against P1, favor C if they are likely good; D only if the chance they are selfish is high enough that avoiding a loss outweighs the welfare C creates for a good opponent.

P6 is unobserved, so cooperate unless evidence suggests they are selfish; cooperation best supports the total payoff of good players. If they are selfish, they are expected to defect, making my defection preferable.
